The documents do not conflict due to outdated information; they are complementary. d1, d3, d5, d6, and d7 all state that many penguin species live in warm climates, while d2 and d4 focus on cold-adaptation mechanisms. These are different facets of the same topic: some species are adapted for warmth, others for cold, and all have thermoregulatory strategies.

The evidence collectively shows that penguins can survive in warm weather, but this ability varies by species. d3 and d6 explicitly state that species like the African and Galapagos penguins live in warm/tropical climates [d3, d6]. d1 and d5 note penguins live in regions with temperatures up to 90°F (32°C) or 100°F above zero [d1, d5]. d2 and d4 detail cold-weather adaptations but do not contradict the warm-climate facts; they are complementary explanations of how different penguins cope with their environments [d2, d4]. d7 adds that Humboldt penguins are comfortable in warm Hawaiian weather [d7]. Together, they provide a complete picture: survival in warm weather is species-dependent and involves specific behavioral and physiological adaptations.

Yes, many penguin species can survive in warm weather. Several sources note that penguins are found in warm climates, with about 14 species living in such areas, including the African, Galapagos, and Humboldt penguins [d3, d6, d7]. They inhabit regions where temperatures can reach 90–100°F (32–38°C) along coasts in South America and Africa [d1, d5]. These warm-weather penguins use adaptations like stretching their flippers to shade their feet and panting to cool down [d3]. However, other species, like Emperor and Adélie penguins, are exclusively adapted to cold Antarctic environments [d4, d7]. Therefore, the answer depends on the species, as penguins have diverse habitats and thermoregulatory strategies.
